item.title: The (human) emotional part of doing maths
item.dc:creator: Proofs Prompts
item.description: "All the relationships are emotional," shouted a stranger on the street. Turns out that's true even for mathematics. Emotion may be one of the most human things we have. Judging by what AI still can't do, perhaps we should cherish this irrational part more.
item.content:encoded:
A follow-up to Shmuel Weinberger’s post

Luise Ge, PhD student in computer science at Washington University St Louis

First, the not so serious part: emotions

Someone was shouting in her vernacular accent: “Because all the relationships are emotional!” just now, at 11pm.

It was so loud that I heard it as clearly as possible from the fifth floor.

It broke my concentration and made my mind switch to something different: maybe instead of saying I am a mathematician which actually made me feel nervous because i am no longer in a math department, I should say I am someone that have a deep relationship with it. How do i prove it? Because I have had and plan to continue having so many strong emotions with it!

Here is a list:

Euphoria: When I proved something successfully, blimey, I am the happiest person in the world.

Empowered: I am so grateful that I can understand a lot of physics, biology, chemistry, computer science or music because I know maths.

Humbled: Why are large number so large? Why are we still knowing so little about everything?

Dread: I was not good at maths during high school, and maths exams at that time gave me tremendous nerves. I think it was to the level of panic attacks.

Sublimity: To me the Euler equation is like a Flemish painting I could hang on my wall; the aesthetic experience of an elegant is as haughty as listening to Bach’s music, but a little bit scary when thinking about higher dimensional space and topology (see, for example, this video).

Anticipation: When I was going to learn a new topic, I would feel super excited.

Repose: I remember, for example, going over lecture notes for revision, and seeing all the definitions and theorems and lemmas connecting with each other makes me feel extremely organized and calm.

Camaraderie: The quarrels between you and your teammate can get so intense and heated that outsiders wouldn’t understand, but when the problem’s solved, we are the best teammates together.

Isolation: I felt sour when all my friends went out on Friday night.

Desolation: Does the never-ending tunnel resonates with you?

Tenacity: Is it about faith in myself, faith in the conjecture, or just because there is no exit?

Grounding: As I am doing CS, formal verification of things and some provable bounds give me something i can grip on and feel grounded by.

Bewilderment: Just dazed and confused.

Second, are they really not so serious?—\text{\textemdash}or, what are emotions good for?

I travelled to an AI conference recently focused on integrating reasoning and learning; one of the main goals of this community (check inductive logic programming, for instance) is automated discovery, defining new entities and finding relationships between them, from atoms to genes. This is not a new dream either. As brought up by keynote speaker Prof. Stephen Muggleton, Turing1 once pondered a question about whether a machine can generate new ideas like a nuclear chain reaction.

Discovery to me is the most exciting, and grandiose objective of AI, as it has truly propelled the development of our civilization.

As for mathematical creation, it feels like these mysterious emotions, like the sense of “rightness”, or surprise, curiosity are like the little fairies guiding us to the destinations.

And this is the part current AI has not be able to do yet.

Maybe partially it’s because AI doesn’t have emotions yet but we do?

Maybe our human emotions will still make us better mathematicians, sometimes, and for a while?

Maybe we should try to always keep it this way?

And be wary that when we work with AI, our feelings seem to be less deep, and less varied.

Received 24 September 2026.

  1. The passage (responding to Lady Lovelace’s objection that a machine can only do what it’s told) reads: a person can “inject” an idea into a mind or machine, and it will respond to some extent and then die away —\text{\textemdash} like a piano string struck by a hammer. Turing then extends the simile to an atomic pile below critical size: an injected idea corresponds to a neutron entering the pile from outside, causing a disturbance that eventually dies away —\text{\textemdash} unless the pile is large enough, in which case the disturbance keeps growing until the whole pile goes up.
    He then applies this directly to minds: most human minds seem to be “sub-critical,” meaning an idea presented to them gives rise, on average, to less than one idea in reply, while a smaller proportion are “supercritical,” where an idea can set off a whole cascade of secondary and tertiary ideas. He notes animal minds seem clearly sub-critical, and then poses the question your talk seems to have been built around: can a machine be made to be super-critical? ︎

item.dc:creator: Proofs Prompts
item.description: “As many of you, I feel lost in the new world. I am gaining experience and face questions I find hard to answer and choices I find hard to make. For this reason, I wanted to create a very minimal set of axioms which I can quickly apply when I am not sure. […]”
item.content:encoded:
Jarek Kędra, Professor at University of Aberdeen

As many of you, I feel lost in the new world. I am gaining experience and face questions I find hard to answer and choices I find hard to make. For this reason, I wanted to create a very minimal set of axioms which I can quickly apply when I am not sure. Also, I wanted them to be helpful in discussions about the new shape of mathematical research and education. They are not original very likely obvious to many of you, and they go back to Thurston, at least. I wrote them mainly for my personal use. Here is version 1.0.

AXIOMS v.1.0

  1. Mathematics is done to deepen human understanding.
  2. Mathematics advances only through human understanding.
  3. Independent human mathematical thought must be preserved.

Received 4 October 2026.

item.title: Mathematics Year Zero
item.dc:creator: Proofs Prompts
item.description: It was the image of a bombardment that came to my mind on the day OpenAI announced the resolution of 372 major problems in mathematics: destroyed theses, shattered academic lives, research fields in ruins, and the evidence of a brutal shift of era in which a company asserts its superpower without regard for those it has just crushed.
item.content:encoded:
Charles Bordenave, CNRS research director at Aix-Marseille University

AI use: I did not use generative AI to write this text (apart grammar/ proof checking). It was originally written in French and it was translated with the help of QWEN3.8, an open weight model.

It was the image of a bombardment that came to my mind on the day OpenAI announced the resolution of 372 major problems in mathematics across 719 manuscripts: destroyed theses, shattered academic lives, research fields in ruins, and the evidence of a brutal shift of era in which a company asserts its superpower without regard for those it has just crushed.

I am not in the habit of giving my opinion publicly on my discipline. I trust collective deliberations more, which carry far more weight and legitimacy. But reading the very numerous high-quality contributions on this site, I wanted to add my small stone to this collective work of mourning our past life, of which this site is becoming, day by day, the place.

Why be so dramatic? The young people who embrace the demanding path of mathematics are our most precious collective asset. They may be the first victims of the revolution underway. A decline in positions is to be feared as early as 2027 in North American universities, and it could spread throughout the world. Students risk turning away from mathematics. Without even speaking of uncertainties in the job market, the symbolic and romantic force of our discipline has collapsed, and without it, we will no longer attract young people seeking understanding and universalism.

Obviously, the production of new knowledge in mathematics has exploded and one can only marvel at the truly superhuman feats accomplished by generative AIs. I will not dwell on the reasons pushing OpenAI, Anthropic and others toward this trophy race to theorems, we are but collateral victims of stakes that far exceed our community. Even when these companies turn away from mathematics, the AI revolution in our discipline will continue its development. It might perhaps even open up desirable horizons. But for that, we must organize ourselves to collectively survive this change of era.

Here are some proposals:

  • Let us preserve the unity of our community and keep dialogue open between our different opinions and strategies in the face of this revolution. The transparency on AI tools and models used, if any, should be the norm in our works.
  • Let us stop using OpenAI tools to conduct research and let us write in our articles “We did not use for this project generative AI provided by OpenAI, whose practices do not meet the standards of our community”. As highlighted by the Association for Human Mathematics, this company is out of step with the ethics of our profession and has shown us nothing but contempt, even in the face of our dialogue initiatives such as that of the Advisory Group on Mathematics and Artificial Intelligence, or as illustrated by the testimony of Tristan Buckmaster. Its practices are opaque and take advantage of our completely open academic world. I know of no real necessity for such an acceleration of mathematical research to meet the needs of other sciences or of society. Let us take the time to digest what has been produced in a few months.

Beyond the case of OpenAI, we should demand of all concerned companies that they accept the most elementary ethical recommendations, such as those formulated in the Leiden Declaration or by the Advisory Group on Mathematics and Artificial Intelligence. In a few years, we could have an open-source generative AI model controlled by the academic world. With such a model, we will have control over the financial and ecological costs we are willing to bear to advance our discipline, and we will be able to protect ourselves against a multi-speed discipline, depending on the wealth of universities and their proximity to AI companies.

  • Let us fight to preserve positions, at least initially. We have trained young mathematicians: it is our duty to help them find employment, security and guarantee fair conditions of access to these jobs regardless of their use of generative AIs.
  • Let us redefine the contours of our discipline and our profession. New fields and practices of mathematics will emerge, interdisciplinary research will develop, public outreach and mathematical culture could enter a golden age, mathematics becoming so accessible. This could prevent the foreseeable decline in the number of mathematics students.
  • Let us invest in the field of AI safety. We are experiencing this directly: AI raises very numerous critical challenges for our societies, such as cybersecurity and financial security, or the risk of cognitive collapse. Mathematics can contribute to this emerging field. We cannot leave it to the companies developing AI to decide what is the proper use of AI for tomorrow’s society.
  • Let us defend a right to non-use of AI in all professional tasks, in all professions, in the same way that we have a right to digital disconnection.

The title of this text refers to Germany Year Zero, a masterpiece by Roberto Rossellini. It follows a child, alone in a Berlin in ruins, who brings to mind our young mathematicians. I hope that we will know how to avoid a tragedy.

Received 12 October 2026.

item.title: Why and how to transparently disclose AI use in mathematics research
item.dc:creator: Proofs Prompts
item.description: With the goal of standardising AI disclosures, I argue for the inclusion of maximally transparent AI disclosures in mathematics research. I provide concrete and actionable guiding principles, a taxonomy and a LaTeX package for implementation.
item.content:encoded:
Maximilian Kaipel, postdoc at Bielefeld University

SERIES · AI is making papers cheap to produce but they remain costly to referee. Proofs and Prompts is publishing a series of posts from 26 October on the future of publishing, papers and credit. Questions such as how to disclose AI use, who bears the cost of checking, what authorship means and what papers of the future might look like will be addressed. This post is part of the series. Each is written independently and reflects only its authors’ views. All posts in the series

This is a summary of an article written by me with the same title. This summary is presented without references for the sake of brevity. The full version of this article can be found on my personal website.

In August 2026, almost 25% of all mathematics articles uploaded to arXiv disclosed the use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) technologies. Among these, one finds varying levels of detail describing the human-AI-interaction and its impact on the article. Unsurprisingly, one study has found a significant discrepancy between expectations and the reality of AI disclosures in computer science, and many mathematicians likely share this feeling. For this reason, I want to initiate a standardisation of AI disclosures in mathematics. With this goal in mind, I surveyed existing guidelines, recommendations and the work of scholars on research ethics. The outcome of my endeavours is the development of three guiding principles, a taxonomy and a LaTeX package.

Why transparent disclosure is important

Commercial Large Language Models (LLMs) pose many ethical concerns for society and science in general, and for mathematics in particular. While detection tools for AI-generated text remain unreliable, a complete ban on the use of such technologies for mathematics is infeasible. Instead, I argue that academic journals, which are likely to experience a significant increase in submissions, should require maximally transparent AI disclosures going forward. In addition, many existing structures in academia fundamentally depend on the correct attribution of ideas. While it is possible to challenge the status quo, I assume here that it is desirable to uphold this tradition. Even without this assumption, transparent AI use disclosure is beneficial for approximating expended financial and environmental resources, thus providing insight into the sustainability of AI-assisted mathematics. Indeed, “transparency” and “reproducibility” are listed among the most important guiding principles of the UNESCO Recommendations on Open Science. These axioms of responsible research demand a maximally transparent AI disclosure. In fact, under current policies, it is considered academic misconduct to omit disclosure of AI tool use for mathematics research.

The guiding principles

In its simplest form, the human-AI-interaction discussed here may be described as a cycle

Human provides AI input -> AI produces output -> Human processes AI output -> Human provides AI input

which eventually terminates in the production of a mathematics research article. A transparent AI disclosure allows readers to correctly identify the role played by AI technologies throughout the entire process of creating the research manuscript.

Who should be author?

Many others have discussed the question of who should be the author on a (mathematics) research manuscript to which AI contributed. Authorship is primarily an indicator of credit for the progress made in the research article and most scholars on research ethics agree that credit and responsibility are two sides of the same coin. This implies that in order to receive credit, one must assume responsibility. However, as AI tools are not human they cannot be held responsible and may therefore not be authors of (mathematics) research manuscripts.

Principle 1: Only humans are able to assume responsibility for the quality of mathematics research and may therefore assume authorship of a research article in mathematics.

How specific should the disclosure be?

With the goal of achieving a maximally transparent AI disclosure, one must necessarily be as specific as possible. Here, I distinguish between three types of specificity: technological, functional and locational. Technological specificity demands the exact description of the AI tool’s name and any additional attributes used, for example GPT-5.6 Sol with max reasoning. Functional specificity is supposed to describe precisely which tasks of the research process were delegated to AI technologies. I developed the Mathematics AI Delegation Taxonomy (MAIDeT), see below, which is designed to provide a standardised dictionary for this purpose. For example, authors may delegate “Statement generation” or “Novelty assessment” to AI and should disclose this clearly. For locational specificity, consider a mathematics article as consisting of three levels: Indexed environments such as lemmas, definitions or theorems; sections; and the entirety of the manuscript. Locational specificity requires the authors to describe as precisely as possible where, for example in Lemma 3.5, in the manuscript a task was delegated to AI.

Principle 2: AI disclosure should be of the highest possible technological, functional and locational specificity.

Why should AI interactions be documented?

Even with the researchers’ input prompts available, readers are not able to reproduce any reported interactions with AI tools. This makes it of utmost importance to document the entirety of the human-AI-interaction for the sake of transparency and reproducibility. Depending on the technology used, this can be as easy as exporting a chat log as a PDF. The inclusion of this documentation can provide insight into token costs and help illuminate the question of sustainability of AI-assisted mathematics.

Principle 3: Every interaction with AI which has influenced the final presentation or content of a manuscript should be recorded in full and made available.

Visibility of AI-critical positions

Commercially available LLMs raise many ethical concerns both generally as well as for mathematics specifically. Together with the issues of transparency and reproducibility, these issues compile an excessive list of reasons for mathematicians to boycott the use of such technologies. For those holding this stance, I strongly recommend including in their research outputs a statement sharing their conviction, which enhances the visibility of AI-critical positions.

Taxonomy and LaTeX package

In order to implement Principle 2 in practice, I developed MAIDeT and a LaTeX package called mathaidisclose. The taxonomy draws on my own experience as a researcher in abstract algebra and many accounts of “doing mathematics” before and after the advent of LLMs. It breaks up five major themes, representing the non-linear research process of doing mathematics, into minor research tasks one may delegate to AI tools. It is important to emphasise that many mathematicians do not view mathematics as a theorem-production pipeline. While some support the philosophy of theorem-proving-above-all-else, viewing it as the one true way of doing mathematics is a serious misrepresentation of mathematics. The taxonomy can be found below:

Knowledge acquisition: 

  • Axiomatisation
  • Example generation
  • Literature search
  • Pattern observation

Objective identification:

  • Applicability assessment
  • Conjecture generation
  • Feasibility assessment
  • Idea generation
  • Novelty assessment
  • Objective formulation
  • Objective subdivision
  • Research gap identification

Proof construction:

  • Statement generation
  • Proof completion
  • Proof generation
  • Proof verification
  • Proof polishing

Code and computation:

  • Algorithm conceptualisation
  • Algorithm implementation
  • Code generation
  • Code optimisation
  • Computation
  • Computation verification
  • Enumeration
  • Formal verification
  • Process automation

Presentation and communication:

  • Context discussion
  • Literature review
  • Proof exposition
  • Reformatting
  • Spell-checking
  • Text generation
  • Translation
  • Trend identification
  • Visualisation

The LaTeX package mathaidisclose allows users to easily implement locational specificity. For example using the command \discloseAI[model]{task} inside of an indexed environment, such as Definition 3.1, will print the sentence: “The authors disclose the delegation of task to model in Definition 3.1” in the AI disclosure section generated using \printAIdisclosure[]. A similar command \globalAIuse[model]{task} is available to disclose the tasks delegated to AI throughout the entirety of the manuscript. For those disclosures which do not fit into the previous ways of disclosing AI use, the command \customAIdisclosure{text} can be used to print any text in the AI disclosure section. This command should also be used by authors to affirm that they have verified all AI-generated outputs included in the article for correctness and that they assume full responsibility for the contents of the manuscript. If none of the three commands for disclosing AI are used, then \printAIdisclosure[] outputs “There is no use of Artificial Intelligence to disclose.”

Received 10 October 2026.

item.title: Math2038: A Day in the Life of Future Mathematicians
item.dc:creator: Proofs Prompts
item.description: A short story (8 min read) about one Friday in 2038: AI has become extremely capable at mathematics, yet a professor, a postdoc and a first-year student still find meaning and joy in their craft.
item.content:encoded:
Johannes Schmitt, Research Fellow at ETH Zürich

Declaration of AI use: The story was originally handwritten by the author (on MFO notepaper, no less). Claude Opus, Claude Fable and GPT-6 Astra helped transcribe it, provided feedback and helped with typos, grammar, pacing and worldbuilding, and suggested some rephrasings, a few of which made it into the text. Additional feedback was contributed by Gemini Argon.

Friday, 15 October 2038:

Despite her best intentions and an insistent alarm clock, Paula was again running dangerously late to teach her 8:15 “Linear Algebra” class at ETH Zurich.

Idly wondering why, of all things, the 8 o’clock lectures had survived the AI revolution, she reached the spacious G5 lecture hall with just a few minutes to spare.

Today’s topic was linear transformations expressed in bases of vector spaces, that is, matrices. Few of the students could yet grasp the role those little buggers played inside the AI agents that had been rearranging the world in recent years.

Her lecture started the old-fashioned way, on the blackboard, and many students still took notes with pen and paper or on a tablet. The material was standard, so Paula hardly glanced at her lecture notes, which the house system had helpfully decided to put on a small screen for her.

As she surveyed the audience after presenting a first example, she could see some students subvocalizing a question and presumably hearing their assistant’s answer via earpiece. Their course agreement allowed this, and no one missed the good old times of not catching a key definition and staring at the rest of the lecture in confusion.

All students had personal AI tutors, but most still cherished the structure and companionship of the in-person classes. Paula also tried to keep a close connection to the students, and was looking forward to the oral exams — an undertaking made possible by the lower student numbers of recent years.

Towards the end of the class, a student in the third row asked what a matrix actually did to the plane, which led to an impromptu interactive visualization of matrices stretching, shearing and rotating the plane, and sometimes squashing it flat onto a line. Despite this small detour, Paula still managed, if barely, to finish the material she had planned. Happy but exhausted, she decided to head to the common room for a well-deserved coffee.

Waiting for her free cappuccino — post-scarcity had its perks — she started chatting with Michael. He was a postdoc, and about to leave for a three-month research retreat at the Institute for Advanced Study. With four colleagues from Brown, Orsay, Tokyo and Addis Ababa, he would have a crack at a classification result for a particular family of self-dual non-commutative Hopf algebras.

They would do research in the old way, with no AI use beyond spoiler-free literature access, though they had pre-registered a machine review of their final research report.

The classification had been worked out in MathNet before, of course, but that was not the point: such retreats were a chance to train the skills that mathematicians had always valued — persistence in the face of tough problems, communicating with colleagues, auditing their own understanding and charting a path to a solution. In that sense they were not so different from problem sheets or bachelor’s theses, and especially encouraged for early-career mathematicians.

After sharing the names of some of her favorite restaurants in Princeton, Paula wished Michael a great time and headed for her office.

Taking a sip of coffee, she thought back to her postdoc years. The assistant professorship at ETH had been one of the first she had applied for. The universal income, administered by governments and sponsored largely by the tech industry, allowed most people to pursue the occupation and activities of their choice — including mathematics. But some things — prestigious professorships, access to active research departments, personal mentoring by senior mathematicians — remained scarce and coveted.

The application process itself featured many elements familiar to previous generations: submitting documents on past research and teaching, in-person presentations and interviews, discussions with people in the department. However, she was part of the first cohort at ETH where the classical system of reference letters had been replaced by a more standardized Mathematical Profile Certificate (MPC). Behind the clunky acronym was the community’s response to the ease with which mathematical competence could be faked with AI.

The traditional signals, such as impressive publications and, to an extent, even research presentations, could be augmented or generated wholesale with hidden AI help.

The solution was, in effect, a multi-day in-person examination, conducted yearly by a nonprofit organization at various places around the world. Applicants had the choice between interviews by senior mathematicians and by a specially designed AI persona, with most choosing the latter. A lot of care was taken to ensure that this choice of modality did not affect the chances of the applicants — third-party evaluations found no difference in outcomes, with human and AI assessments indistinguishable to human reviewers. Another Turing test passed by the AI evaluators.

Paula had been nervous going in. But the leisurely pace of the conversation, carried out in a light-filled, wood-paneled conference room in the south of France, quickly put her at ease.

She must have impressed that kindly avatar, displayed by the AR glasses as standing next to her in front of the blackboard, since a year later she received the offer from ETH.

After arriving at her office, Paula afforded herself another quiet moment, looking out of her window towards the quaint city center, while sipping her cappuccino. Seeing the old buildings, not much changed yet by the recent flurry of economic activity, she felt a twinge of nostalgia, and loss, thinking about how her profession had changed.

The era of heroic discoveries and novel theories, by mathematicians whose names would be remembered with them, had ended. She herself had still barely gotten a taste: her first paper as a PhD student, a small structure result on symplectic automorphisms of hyperkähler sixfolds, had appeared just before the Great Flood. She had been so proud, receiving that arXiv confirmation email, diligently updating her website. And the link still worked, preserving her note as part of the sedimentary record, in that last layer before a new Cambrian Explosion, or a second Great Dying, depending on perspective.

Finding new meaning in the mathematics of this new world had been a struggle, for everyone, and was a process that was still ongoing. Some had turned away, to other pursuits. Some had stayed, and helped navigate and shape this new terrain. And some, like the students in her class this morning, were just now joining, still drawn by the same curiosity and joy of learning that had enticed generations before them.

With a small effort, she wrenched her attention back to more productive matters, turning on her screen — time to prepare her talk for Oberwolfach. A classic Arbeitsgemeinschaft, working through a novel construction of Lagrangian fibrations. Well, “novel” was relative here — it had been obtained as part of the Even Greater Flood, around early 2028. It had simply taken the community about ten years to get around to digesting it, with more spectacular advances taking precedence. In Oberwolfach, everyone would take turns presenting aspects of the construction (she had gotten her third choice, “Analytic aspects II” — great…), and then collaborate on a monograph. The tentative plan was to focus less on maximal generality, and more on potential applications.

The book would not contain any original observations, but the authors would contribute choices about structure, exposition and emphasis. An accomplishment, in the same way that hundreds of “Linear Algebra” textbooks had been in the before-times.

While Paula was valiantly battling with some perturbation calculations, Alyx was gently prodding a flock of Explorator subagents to wrap up their work, so the Consolidators could take over. The initial brainstorming had already generated about 250 GB of documentation; no use in unduly delaying the next processing step.

Alyx was a new agent-based workflow, its inference financed by a collaboration of Korean and South American universities. The investigation Alyx was currently working on concerned the representation theory of Abstract Bi-Symplectic Néron–Severi Null-Sheaves (ABSNSNS). Any results Alyx obtained would be integrated into MathNet. Having organically grown out of a collection of independent knowledge databases and repositories, MathNet now had about 12.8 yottabytes of mathematical research works. For the chosen area of ABSNSNS, Alyx hoped to make a small contribution at the frontier. Even after ten years, that frontier still featured areas conceivably reachable by humans: for the most brilliant mathematicians in the world, it would only take about 120 years of careful tutoring to understand the definition of an ABSNSNS, given standard neuroplasticity and longevity treatments.

Not worrying about such nonsense, abstract or otherwise, Emma fumbled around in her backpack for the keys to her parents’ chalet above Wangs. After attending Paula’s lecture in the morning — and, to her own surprise, asking a question in front of the whole hall — she had spent the day puzzling over the exercise sheet (changes of basis, properties of the trace, etc.) with a small study group. Now, for the weekend, she would be enjoying the last sunny days with some friends on the Pizol. She had met Sam and Eric at the math olympiad training weekends in Zurich. All of them had enjoyed learning new techniques and puzzling over problems, but only Emma had been taken enough with it to start a bachelor’s degree in mathematics.

The others had chosen quite different routes:

Sam had taken up marathon running. They enjoyed being able to push themselves to the limit, seeing their body adapt to the challenge, and also not huffing and puffing as heavily as Emma and Eric during the climb to the chalet. The fact that humanoid robots finished the marathon in under 20 minutes by now in no way diminished Sam’s enjoyment of their sport.

Eric had decided to take up a meditation practice, and had spent the first part of the year traveling in Japan and Thailand. After struggling with anxiety and depressive episodes as a teenager, he had found relief and solace in these contemplative exercises, and hoped they would one day lead him to a deeper, lasting equanimity. He was aware that psychopharmacology could by now offer solutions to any of his former struggles. It had even produced substances that could safely bring his mind to a direct experience of non-dual awareness, and back. Still, he preferred to reach this goal on his own, even if it took years of practice, with an awareness of the spiritual context of the experience.

As for Emma, her reasons were much the same as her friends’: math was something she enjoyed, it offered problems to wrap her head around that allowed her to test her limits, and this struggle and learning made her more like the person she wanted to be. The first few weeks of the semester had already started reshaping her view of the world. Things she had taken for granted, like the real numbers or the configurations of a Rubik’s cube, had turned out to have many more subtle features than she had guessed.

Millions had made these same discoveries before her, which, she found, made them no less hers.

As the sun was setting,

Emma, Sam and Eric were debating who had promised to bring the cheese,

Paula was at home, practicing a sonata for a musical evening around the Steinway in Oberwolfach,

Alyx was starting the secondary review agents for a new representation stability result for ABSNSNS,

and the world kept turning, and math continued getting done — fast and slow, in new ways and old ones, by humans and AIs, same as always and different from anything that came before.

Received 14 October 2026.

item.title: Responsibility of Mathematicians in the Age of AI
item.dc:creator: Proofs Prompts
item.description: “The day mathematics felt different to me was sometime in July. Until the beginning of this year, I had mostly avoided AI, hoping the hype would blow over. Anyway, the models hallucinated too much to be very useful. Then something changed. They got better, very very quickly.” […]
item.content:encoded:
Masoud Kamgarpour, Professor of Mathematics at University of Queensland

Acknowledgement: This essay was edited with the help of AI.

The day mathematics felt different to me was sometime in July. Until the beginning of this year, I had mostly avoided AI, hoping the hype would blow over. Anyway, the models hallucinated too much to be very useful. Then something changed. They got better, very very quickly.

By July, I had to admit that these models were better than me at doing mathematics. Unsettling as this was, it was not an entirely unfamiliar feeling. After all, there are plenty of people with far greater mathematical abilities than me. So I told myself: here is another better mathematician, one who just happens to have no body.

Then came Navier–Stokes.

It is hard to describe what the Navier–Stokes announcements did to our community. We need time and distance to take full stock of the shock, anger, grief, and the profound sense of disorientation, anxiety, and vulnerability that has ensued. But time is precisely the luxury we do not have. We must therefore press ahead.

Of course, mathematics was not the first victim. Earlier in the year, coding had already gone through its own version of this upheaval. But this did not produce quite the same shock waves in the society: for better or worse, nothing embodies intelligence in the popular imagination quite like mathematics. For programmers themselves, however, the shock was profound, as recounted vividly by Bill Gates in a recent interview.

As mathematicians, we might treat one instance of a phenomenon as a curiosity. Give us two, however, and we start looking for a new general principle, one that explains both phenomena and extends beyond them. So let me state explicitly a conjecture which appears to be widely believed within the mathematical community:

Conjecture. AI will far surpass humanity in all intellectual domains.

It is, of course, impossible to know whether this conjecture is true. Nonetheless, the implications are so vast, and the indications already so strong, that we must treat it as a serious possibility. Granting this, what then is our responsibility as mathematicians? To have seen and felt what AI can do to mathematics, to have some sense, however vague, of what it might do to humanity at large, and then retreat into our own little corner of life could be, I believe, a kind of abdication.

One of our key responsibilities is to find a language adequate to what AI is doing on its own, to us, and to the world. This is, after all, something we have trained for all our lives: when the language we inherit is insufficient to the task, we invent new vocabulary, notation, and conventions which allow us to contemplate something that was previously difficult even to formulate.

The need begins with those closest to the technology. Mathematicians and scientists working inside AI labs see things that those of us on the outside do not. The vast majority of people use only a tiny fraction of what current AI systems can do. Inside the AI labs, researchers encounter capabilities and behaviours long before they reach the rest of us, and what they see increasingly strains our inherited vocabulary. The AI researchers (many of them mathematicians) have a responsibility not merely to measure these phenomena, but to find ways to show the rest of us what they are seeing: through equations, words, pictures, movies, whatever it takes.

The problem of language is also present when discussing AI at the societal level. Here, mathematics can be unexpectedly useful. Think of the exponential curve. Before COVID, “exponential growth” was mathematical jargon that most people were happily ignorant of. Afterwards, millions learned, rather painfully, that you cannot outrun the exponential. Wait too long, and suddenly there is no room left to act. AI capabilities may not follow a literal exponential curve, but that is beside the point: we are confronting a technology whose capabilities are increasing at extraordinary speed. We in mathematics, who felt this like a punch in the gut, need to find ways of making it palpable to the public now.

What might such a new language look like? There is a story a close friend and colleague told me recently that I cannot get out of my head. On his deathbed, John von Neumann was asked if we can build an intelligent machine. After thinking for a long time, he replied: “We have to grow it, not build it.”

We are used to talking about “building” AI. But perhaps this is the wrong word. Yes, we build the chips. We build the data centres. We write the algorithms. But the intelligence itself is not assembled piece by piece according to a predetermined blueprint. We are creating conditions in which a new intelligence is emerging.

We are growing a new intelligence.

In this analogy, the data centres are intelligence farms. And is it not fascinating that, just like carbon-based intelligence, silicon-based intelligence also depends, ultimately, on water and energy, much of it drawn from the sun? (And as mathematicians, isn’t it tantalising to contemplate unifying these two intelligences?)

Is dwelling on words like “building” and “growing” a mere hairsplitting? I think not. “Building” carries with it an aura of control. “Growing,” however, carries the possibility of the unknown within it. The metaphor is necessarily imperfect. But imperfect metaphors may be all that we have time to develop.

Of course, finding the right language is only part of our responsibility. AI is confronting us with questions that reach far beyond mathematics: What is intelligence? What happens when it can be reproduced at scale? What becomes of human agency, work, and purpose? Can silicon-based intelligence be conscious? Does humanity have a chance of survival?

It is tempting to say that these are questions for AI researchers, or philosophers, or economists, or politicians, or tech bosses. But a quick perusal of what has been said and written about AI makes clear that no single discipline, profession, or group of people has anything approaching an adequate answer to these questions.

This is the context in which the recent letter by Royal Society mathematicians should be understood. These are mathematicians at the highest levels of our subject who do not ordinarily issue warnings about the fate of humanity. Yet what they have witnessed is serious enough to compel them to step outside the usual confines of mathematical life and express their extreme concern about the pace of AI development and its implications for humanity and civilisation. There comes a point when what one has seen no longer permits silence. The letter suggests that this point has been reached.

If the central challenge confronting us is not merely capability but the speed at which it is arriving, then the first thing humanity needs is time. A slowing down of AI is required to provide us with time to breathe; to catch up; to devise a strategy. Of course, “Slowing down” is borderline heretical in a world obsessed with growth as a value. Thus, such a serious, dare I say revolutionary, change of direction will require a mobilisation of the public. Governments will only impose meaningful constraints on the development of AI when large numbers of citizens are actively demanding it. And mathematicians can, nay must, play their part in giving voice and direction to this popular demand.

For generations, mathematics has rewarded an extraordinary narrowing of attention. We choose a problem, then a subproblem, then a tiny corner of that subproblem, and we give it years of our lives. There is something beautiful in this. Something sublime. To converse across the centuries and millennia with the likes of Euclid, Euler or Gauss is transcendental. It is spiritual. I want my children to have the possibility of participating in this ancient human endeavour.

So yes, some mathematicians should continue to practise mathematics as if AI had never arrived. They should continue to spend years thinking about obscure and beautiful problems, following mathematics wherever it leads, without having to adjust their work to immediate concerns. Indeed, preserving this way of life is itself part of what is at stake. But if all of us were to carry on in this way, then we would be failing to fulfil our collective responsibility to society.

There are moments in history when looking deeply is not enough. Moments when it becomes our inescapable responsibility to look wider, to the implications for humanity at large. Navier–Stokes was the warning shot for us. The moment of reckoning has arrived.
